text:
﻿If you're looking to make a 360 virtual 
tour using a camera like the Insta360 X5,

following the wrong workflow can waste both time 
and money. Using the wrong shooting settings,

editing in the wrong software, as well as 
producing low-quality images that make your

work look amateur. But never fear. In this video, 
I'll show you how to achieve the best quality

possible with the X5 while wasting the least 
amount of time, as well as showing you the best

free software you can use at every stage of the 
editing journey. Consider this video a taste of

the value you'll find inside my full Virtual Tour 
Pro course, which will teach you everything else

you need to know to create professional 
virtual tours that you can charge for,

even if you're using a consumer 360 camera like 
the X5. If you're curious, I'll link it below.

Let’s start with gear. And in this tutorial, 
I'll be using the X5. Big thanks goes out

to Insta360 for sponsoring this video. If 
you haven't picked yourself up an X5 yet,

I will link it below, and it may even come with 
a freebie or two. The only other thing you need,

really, aside from the camera, is a monopod 
of some sort. Here I'm using a combination of

two different things because I was travelling. I 
wanted to pack light. So, I've used a selfie stick

from the Best 360 Monopod, and I've combined that 
with the Insta360 all-purpose tripod. And since

all accessories usually have a 1/4-inch tripod 
thread, either male or female, most things are

going to be compatible with most other things.
However, if you are looking to invest,

I'd recommend something like the Bushman Monopod 
Pro on the higher end, or the Best 360 Monopod on

the lower end. Whatever you get, you'll just want 
to make sure that the camera extends to eye level,

which is the most natural height to view it from.
But before we get started shooting, first it's

really important to make your space presentable. 
So hopefully the location you're shooting is

already somewhat neat, but you will want to do a 
once-over of the rooms you shoot just to make sure

everything is neat and tidy, including fluffing 
up pillows, getting rid of garbage bins, and

anything else that is cluttering the room. You’ll 
also want to open all doors within the location

so it's easy to navigate from room to room later 
through having a clear visual line of sight. Also,

if you've got windows with curtains, you will want 
to open them as far as possible to let as much

natural light into the room as you can. This will 
help the camera expose the inside of the room far

better. Another thing that helps a lot is turning 
on the internal lights of the room. Even if it is

during the day, it will make a difference.
Next, it's time to turn the camera on and

set our settings. The first thing you want to do 
after navigating to photo mode is bringing up the

resolution screen and just double-checking 
that you have it set to 72 megapixels,

as well as setting the self-timer, which 
will give you a few seconds to go and hide

once you've pressed the shutter button. 
For that, I'd recommend five seconds.

Now, the number one challenge when shooting 360 
photos at an interior location is trying to expose

the outside and the light coming in through the 
windows, since at most locations it's going to

be far brighter outside than it is inside. And 
this produces exposure challenges where you have

two very different types of lighting that you're 
trying to capture in the same shot. And for this

reason, it's important not to leave the X5 
on the standard photo mode. So, up the top

here you'll see there's an HDR photo option, and 
here you can set it to either HDR photo on or AEB,

which refers to auto-exposure bracketing.
Now, many people will make the case for

shooting in bracketing because this is how many 
traditional real estate photographers capture high

dynamic range scenes. However, with the X5 it's a 
different story. Here's what the two options look

like side by side. And at first, you'll notice 
that the bracketing shot has more contrast and

may seem sharper at first, but it also comes 
with introducing a lot more noise and visual

imperfections into the image. If you look at the 
handles of the HDR shot versus the handles with

a bracketing shot, they are easily sharper on 
the left-hand side. Also, all surfaces on the

left-hand side are smoother than the right. And 
this is because bracketing combines several photos

together into one shot. And with that, the quality 
around the high-contrast areas deteriorates,

making straight lines less straight.
And while the in-built HDR is pretty aggressive

with the noise reduction, it still looks better, 
in my opinion, than the bracketing. Bracketing

also struggles a lot more with textures. Like 
here on this bedhead, it has a really bad case of

coloured moiré, and that's going to be practically 
unfixable. Also, bracketing takes a lot longer to

shoot. Here on set, I did a side by side, and my 
HDR photo was taken in just seconds, whereas the

bracketing took a whole minute for just one 
single photo. And that time is really going

to add up, especially with bigger locations.
So, for best image quality and fastest shooting

workflow, I'd recommend turning HDR on. Then 
you'll also want to turn PureShot Plus RAW on,

which will create a backup RAW file that 
you can use in case of emergency where you

may have messed up your exposure somehow, and 
will be much easier for you to fix overblown

highlights and crushed shadows. However, 
most of the time it shouldn't come to that.

Now, in regards to how many shots you should take 
per room, the simple answer I'm going to give you

is one. Assuming you're shooting an interior like 
a hotel, a house, a business, something with an

average-sized room. Don't forget the goal is not 
to create a Google Street View-type experience,

but to just take one money shot per room. That is 
unless the room is substantially big enough that a

second photo justifies a very different change 
in perspective, and therefore another photo.

So, in this big open room here, I do have 
two distinct areas. Over there I've got the

living room, and on this side there's a dining 
and kitchen area. So therefore, I think two

photos is justified. However, for other rooms, 
like bedrooms, this is a much smaller room,

and there's really only one perspective I can take 
here, and that's here in front of the bed. So,

I don't need a second photo. Same 
with bathrooms, hallways, and so on.

Just remember, though, you've got to have a line 
of sight to your previous photo. So, if I'm taking

one out here, I've got a clear line of sight 
to this photo here that I'm going to take in

this spot. So therefore, when I piece this virtual 
tour together, the navigation is going to be easy.

It will look like this. And vice versa. Same with 
here. So, I can obviously see the next point that

I'll navigate to in the tour. So when people click 
on the little hotspot over here, it will go like

this, and there'll be nothing blocking the way.
Now, in terms of where you place your monopod,

chances are you're going to be looking at a floor 
like this with a tile or a carpet with a pattern.

And this can be problematic, especially if you're 
planning on removing your tripod later in editing.

So, if you're able to, I'd recommend placing the 
monopod and tripod right in the middle of a tile

as opposed to covering the lines, because 
this is going to cause obvious stitching

errors and be a nightmare to edit out, whereas 
this is going to be so much easier to work with.

Also, as it goes with most 360 cameras, the 
sides of the camera have the least sharpness. So,

I'd recommend pointing them towards any part 
of your scene that isn't that important,

like an empty wall or maybe a window 
frame, so the front of the lens has a full,

clear view of the more important details that 
you actually want to capture in both directions.

All right, camera's set up and ready to go. 
My self-timer is on, so it's time to shoot.

My plan is to run and hide behind the corner 
there. And I've given myself five seconds

to do that. So, let's do it. There we go.
Okay, I think we're good. And yes, we are.

Now I can move to the next point, which is going 
to be at least six feet in this direction. Let's

move the monopod. And I'm going to put this as 
central as I can in this little lounge room area,

so it really does have a highlight of 
different things and a substantially

different viewpoint to what we just saw.
Before I press the button, though,

one thing I want to point out is that you always 
need to look out for reflections. Even if you

don't have an obvious mirror, there are windows, 
there are TVs, and these are reflective. And

as you can see, I can actually see the camera 
and monopod right there in the TV reflection.

So that could be an issue. So therefore, that's 
going to influence exactly where I place this

monopod. So perhaps I need to move it just a 
little bit back so it minimises that reflection.

Now, there are going to be some situations 
where this is unavoidable, like in bathrooms

with lots of mirrors and there's just 
nowhere to hide. If that's the case,

then yeah, we absolutely can fix this in 
editing, which I'll show you in a bit.

However, rule of thumb is that if you can fix it 
while you're here on location, you should, because

it's going to save you editing time, and this 
can add up if you've got a lot of photos to fix.

Now, my final shooting tip is that before 
you leave your location, to review a couple

of your photos just to make sure you didn't 
mess anything up. You can do this either on

the camera body itself or your phone. And you'll 
just want to take a look at the shots in 360 just

to make sure you didn't mess up the exposure or 
there isn't anything in shot you didn't intend,

because this is your chance to fix it if you 
did. You're not going to have a second chance,

especially if you've got a location for a limited 
time. So, always do this before you leave.

All right, that's a wrap. Well done. Now it's time 
for us to edit our shots using a variety of free

programs. The first one you want to use, which 
you probably already own, is Insta360 Studio.

Here I've got my first shot, and that looks 
great. The exposure is really good, and I'm happy

with the composition. And simply by importing 
these shots here on the left-hand side, the

stitching process is now complete. That was easy.
Now, you'll notice here on the left-hand side that

we've got two versions of each photo, and that 
is because one is a JPEG and one is a RAW shot,

aka a DNG. However, we're going to stick with 
the JPEGs here since I'm happy with how these

turned out and I don't need to use the DNG.
So, the next step I'd recommend you do, and it's

potentially one that can be done here on Insta360 
Studio, is colour correction. So, by clicking

Media Processing here up the top right, this will 
open up a colour correction menu. And if you want

to keep things as simple as possible without using 
an external colour correction software, then you

really can do it here and get decent results.
Now, ultimately it's going to depend what your

shot looks like as to which sliders you use. But 
with virtual tours, I always like to drag the

highlights slider down because that generally 
represents the window area, and it will just

help get the brightest highlights under control. 
As you can see, it's not a massive difference,

but it is noticeable. Next, I'm going to increase 
the contrast just a little bit to make the scene

pop a bit more. And finally, I'm going to boost 
the vibrance, which will selectively increase the

colour saturation of colours that aren't already 
highly saturated. And I'm pretty happy with that.

Here's the before. Here's the after. It's not a 
massive difference, but thankfully the camera did

a pretty good job to start with. Therefore, 
not a lot of colour correction was needed.

However, in other scene types, like this bathroom 
here, you may need to do more extreme colour

correction, since this is feeling a bit flat. 
So I'd probably go a little bit higher with the

contrast and make other changes that are specific 
to this room. So, use your gut instinct here. And

if you don't want to do any colour correction 
at all, that's also okay, because generally I've

found that the images straight out of the camera 
are good enough, especially if you're just doing

it as a personal project. There's no need to 
spend that extra time if you don't want to.

Now, one thing that I want to point out with 
colour correction is that if you've got, say,

a really big room and you've taken lots of shots 
in it, and you know that you're going to be colour

correcting all of those shots in the exact same 
way, well, if these are your colour correction

adjustments, what you want to do is head down 
to batch settings. By default, it will select

everything here. It's basically saying that all of 
these will apply to this batch. Then, if you click

next, you can now navigate to your other shots and 
select the others and then apply in batches. Now,

when I navigate to the other shot, you'll 
see that the exact same colour adjustments

were applied. Definitely a time-saver.
Once all of your edits have been made here

in Insta360 Studio, next we're going to export 
them. And instead of doing it one by one here

on the left-hand side, if you select the first one 
that you want to export and then on your keyboard

hold down Command or Control and then select the 
next one, as well as all the others you want to

export. Now we're going to head up to Export. But 
don't make this mistake of leaving it on Export

Reframe Photo, because this refers to only the 
window you see here, which is the reframe version

of the 360 photo. Instead, we're going to choose 
Export 360 Photo at Original Resolution. And you

want to keep Automatic Horizon Leveling on. Choose 
your save location and then hit Start Export.

Now, one cool thing that I want to point out that 
is a feature of Insta360 Studio is if we look

down, you can see the tripod. And obviously that 
doesn't look great. But here, if you click this

stamp icon here, you can add a custom nadir, which 
essentially means that you can replace the bottom

circle of the image with another static image. 
And here you'll find some Insta360 watermarks.

But if you scroll down, you'll find an Add 
Custom option. And here you can import your

own logo to show up at the bottom. So here I've 
created this logo as a circular PNG in Canva.

I'm going to click OK. And now I can increase or 
decrease the size, but the goal essentially is to

cover this tripod enough. And that has done it. 
You can also rotate it if you like. And look at

that — our tripod is now covered with a logo.
This won't be for everyone. Not every client

you work for is going to be okay with having 
a logo in shot, especially yours. So I'd only

recommend doing this with personal projects. 
However, this is not the only way to get rid

of the tripod. The other way is using the free 
Affinity software, which I'll link below, which

was formerly a paid photo editor that was a great 
alternative to Photoshop that had 360 editing

capabilities. And then Canva bought it and made it 
completely free for anyone to download and use.

So, I've just dragged and dropped one of my photos 
here into Affinity. And as you can see, this is

the equirectangular view, aka the non-360 view. To 
convert this to 360 so we can remove that tripod,

you want to choose Pixel, then Live Projection, 
Equirectangular. And now we can scroll around

this image as an interactive 360 photo. And I'm 
honing in now on this tripod. But first, I want to

get in nice and close. So I'm going to adjust my 
field of view so it's as zoomed in as it can get.

Next, on the left-hand side right here is an 
option called the Inpainting Brush Tool. If

you click that, this is going to be our magic 
paintbrush that eliminates the tripod. So if

you carefully paint over it and try not to 
spill too far into the rest of the image.

That looks pretty good. And now, as soon as 
I let my mouse go, in just seconds Affinity

removes the tripod. And that's done a great job. 
It's matched the pattern of the carpet, and I

don't even need to do another single stroke.
Now, you can get rid of other things in your

image, obviously, like this dot on the floor. If 
you've got any messy surfaces, you can clean them

up. And if you want to look around your image 
again, just go Pixel, Live Projection, then

Remove. This returns us to the equirectangular 
view. And you probably remember from before we had

that monopod reflection on the TV. So I'm going to 
repeat the exact same process as before. This time

I'm going to point the viewpoint at the TV. I'll 
zoom right in, Inpainting Brush Tool, and I'm just

going to paint over this line, and it's gone.
Now, that was totally not necessary, by the way.

I think I did a pretty good job hiding it to 
begin with. But if you are in a room with a

big mirror that makes it unavoidable to see 
the camera reflection, this tool is going to

be so valuable. Just make sure that once you're 
done editing, you go out the same way you came

in through Pixel, Live Projection, Remove. And 
this returns us to the equirectangular view.

Now, Affinity is also a colour correction 
software. So if you did want to do some

more advanced colour correction, you can 
absolutely do it here. However, to keep things

simple in this video, I'm going to leave it.
Now, all we need to do is export our image.

And to do that, head up to the top and go File, 
then down to Export. Export. You'll choose JPEG,

Best Quality, and don't touch 
anything else. And now export.

You can learn more by following the link below.
Now, speaking of virtual tour software, the number

one platform I recommend if you're a beginner

inside this software, you can do everything you

for any type of subscription. While I do have

paid tiers here, these are optional, and you can

free using most features of the software.
Anyway, once you've made yourself a Panoee

account, you'll be directed to your home 
dashboard, which will look something like

this. And we're going to select New Project at the 
top right. We're going to give our tour a name, a

brief description, and a category. And let's go.
From here, the process is really simple. You just

upload your 360 images, then click the ones you 
want to import and choose Submit. And now it's

a pretty straightforward process to build the 
virtual tour. To connect two shots together,

you can just click on the left-hand 
side and drag one into the middle

window. And that will automatically create 
a hotspot that navigates to this shot here,

which you can rename, change the hotspot style, 
move it around so it's perfectly positioned,

and rinse and repeat with your other photos.
If you want to learn my entire workflow inside

Panoee, inside this video here I'll show you 
everything you need to do from start to finish,

so you can import your Insta360 X5 shots and
